title: The Last First: Grace, Greatness, and a Ransom
summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who pays workers hired late in the day the same wage as those who worked all day, and defends his generosity. On the road to Jerusalem he predicts his death and resurrection a third time. When the mother of James and John asks for places of honor for her sons, Jesus teaches that greatness in his kingdom is service, as the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. Leaving Jericho, he gives sight to two blind men who follow him.
story: The chapter continues the conversation that ended chapter 19, where Peter asked what the disciples would receive for leaving everything. The parable of the vineyard answers that the kingdom's rewards are given by grace, not calculated by length of service. The disciples still don't grasp it: immediately after Jesus' most detailed prediction of his suffering, two of them seek the highest seats. Jesus' reply gathers up the whole teaching of this section of Matthew into one sentence about the Son of Man who came to serve. The chapter ends at Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem, with two blind men who see and follow. The next chapter begins the entry into the city.
historical:
The route from Perea to Jerusalem crossed the Jordan near Jericho and climbed some 3,000 feet up through the Judean wilderness to the city, which is why the Gospels speak of going up to Jerusalem. Jericho in Jesus' day was a prosperous oasis town where Herod the Great had built a winter palace, a short distance from the ancient mound of the Old Testament city. That there were two sites may help explain why Mark 10:46 places the healing as Jesus left Jericho and Luke 18:35 as he approached it. Mark names one blind man, Bartimaeus; Matthew, as in 8:28, has two.

Jesus' third prediction adds details not given before: he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, and crucified. Only the Roman governor could impose crucifixion in Judea, so the prediction implies both Jewish and Roman involvement, as chapters 26 and 27 relate. James, one of the two brothers, was later executed by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), the first of the twelve to die for his faith. In Mark 10:35-45 the brothers make the request themselves; Matthew has their mother make it, though Jesus answers the sons. Comparing Matthew 27:56 with Mark 15:40, some suggest their mother was named Salome, but this is not certain.
cultural:
Day laborers gathered in the marketplace at dawn, hoping to be hired. They lived close to poverty, and a day without work could mean a day without food for a family. A denarius was the usual wage for a day's labor. The law of Moses required employers to pay laborers before sundown (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), which is why the foreman pays in the evening. The hours are counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon, and the eleventh about five, an hour before work ended. In verse 15 the landowner asks, literally, whether the worker's eye is evil because he himself is good; the evil eye was a common expression for envy and stinginess.

In the Old Testament the cup often stood for the destiny God assigns, most often the cup of his wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15), and the right and left hand of a king were the places of highest honor. A ransom (lutron) was the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner of war, or a person whose life was forfeit. Beggars sat by the roads near city gates, and a crowd accompanying a famous teacher would see their shouting as a nuisance.
literary: The parable of the vineyard workers (verses 1 to 16), found only in Matthew, is framed by the saying about the last being first (19:30 and 20:16). Its drama depends on the order of payment: by paying the last first, the owner makes sure the first workers see what the latecomers receive. The story ends with the owner's question, not the workers' answer, leaving the hearer to respond. The chapter then sets side by side the third passion prediction (verses 17 to 19) and the request for honor (verses 20 to 28), the same pattern as in chapters 16 and 17: each time Jesus speaks of his death, the disciples misunderstand. The healing of the blind men (verses 29 to 34) closes the section begun in 16:21 on a note of hope. Unlike the disciples who seek seats, the blind men seek sight, and when they receive it, they follow.

outline.t: The parable of the workers in the vineyard
The third prediction of death and resurrection
The request of Zebedee's sons: greatness as service
Two blind men receive sight at Jericho

doctrines.note: Verse 28 is one of the Gospels' clearest statements of the meaning of Jesus' death: he gives his life as a ransom for many, a price paid to set others free. Christians have developed this in more than one way, emphasizing liberation from sin and evil powers, or Christ's taking the penalty others owed, but the verse itself stresses that his death is a costly act of service in the place of many.

The landowner's generosity pictures God's grace: those who come late receive the same gift as those who came early, because the gift depends on the giver's goodness, not the worker's merit. The complaint of the first workers shows how grace offends those who think in terms of wages.

Jesus forbids his followers to exercise authority as Gentile rulers do. In his community greatness is measured by service and the first place belongs to whoever takes the place of a slave, after the pattern of the Son of Man himself.

words.note: Lutron, ransom, the price paid to release a slave or captive. It appears in the New Testament only here and in the parallel Mark 10:45. The phrase for many echoes Isaiah 53:11-12, where the Servant bears the sin of many. The text does not say to whom the ransom was paid, and Christian theologians have debated the question since early centuries.

Diakonos, servant, one who waits on others, especially at tables. The related verb diakoneo appears in verse 28: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The word later came to name an office in the church (deacon), but here it describes the posture of every disciple.

Poterion, cup. Jesus asks the brothers whether they can drink the cup he is about to drink, meaning his suffering and death. He will pray in Gethsemane that this cup might pass from him (26:39), and at the Last Supper the cup becomes the sign of his blood of the covenant (26:27-28).

Denarion, denarius, a Roman silver coin that was a standard day's wage for a laborer. Every worker in the parable receives exactly one. The equal payment is the parable's scandal and its point: God's gift is not measured out by hours worked.

christ: The chapter's summit is Jesus' description of his own mission in verse 28. The Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 to whom all nations were to give service, reverses the picture: he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. That combines Daniel's glorious Son of Man with Isaiah 53's suffering Servant who bears the sins of many, and it explains why the one who will sit on the glorious throne (19:28) must first drink the cup of suffering. The places at his right and left will be seen again at the cross, where two criminals are crucified one on his right and one on his left (27:38). The blind men who call him Son of David and receive sight show what it looks like to recognize the Messiah rightly, and they follow him on the road to Jerusalem.

hard.q: Isn't the landowner in the parable unfair to the workers who labored all day?
hard.a: Most readers instinctively side with the first workers. They worked twelve hours through the heat and received what the latecomers received for one. The landowner's reply is that he has done them no wrong: they agreed to a denarius and received it. Their complaint is not that they were cheated but that others were treated generously. Interpreters draw several lessons. Some read the parable in its setting after Peter's question in 19:27, as a warning to the disciples not to think of the kingdom as a system of wages in which those who have given up more deserve more. Others read it in the context of Jesus' ministry, where tax collectors and sinners entering the kingdom late offended those who had kept the law all their lives, or in the context of Matthew's church, where Gentiles came in alongside Jewish believers. Many see in it the Christian conviction that salvation is a gift of grace equally given, not earned by length or quality of service. The parable does not teach that employers today may ignore justice for workers; the owner in fact pays everyone at least a full day's wage. It asks the hearer whether they can rejoice when grace goes to someone else.

questions: Which workers in the parable do you identify with most, and why? What would it take to rejoice at the landowner's generosity toward others?
James and John wanted greatness, and Jesus redefined it as service. What would greatness as Jesus defines it look like in your home, work, or church?
Jesus asked the blind men, “What do you want Me to do for you?” How would you answer him today?
